_comment: The files under website/atlas/ that scripts/build-atlas-pages.py must NEVER delete or overwrite.
Two kinds: hand-written 'spine' sheets (class="spine") that exist nowhere in data/repertoire.js,
and small meta-refresh stubs kept so URLs already shared keep working.
Detect drift with:  grep -l 'class="spine"' website/atlas/*.html   and   grep -l 'http-equiv="refresh"' website/atlas/*.html
A hand-written sheet MUST also be pinned open — otherwise the build would print 'Not open yet' on a page that already carries the full research, which is a lie on the page itself.

hubCards.blurb: Nobody's country decides whether you're qualified to cook at sea — the flag on the transom does, and it usually asks for less than the schools do. A trade, not a tradition: no master, no workshop, no line of teachers. It passes between chefs who overlap for a season, aboard.
hubCards.school: Anchor & Apron — Cara Whiteman & Amber Colle
hubCards.why: Two experienced yacht chefs who came off the boats to teach their own trade, on published dates, with three days and nights aboard a catamaran. The craft has no lineage to inherit — this is people who do the job, teaching it.

coffee-and-barista.p: Coffee the plant comes from the mountain forests of south-western Ethiopia, where arabica still grows wild. The barista’s craft was born much later, and in Italy. In 1884 Angelo Moriondo of Turin patented the machine that led to espresso; at the start of the twentieth century the Milanese inventor Luigi Bezzera built one that made a single cup to order; and in Milan in 1947 Achille Gaggia’s lever pushed water through the grounds hard enough to raise a crema. That cup is espresso, and the person who pulls it is the barista. Today the craft is most alive in Melbourne, in a country whose cafés were strong enough that Starbucks closed 61 of its 84 Australian stores in 2008, and where Jack Simpson of Axil Coffee Roasters won the 2025 World Barista Championship against competitors from more than fifty countries.

chocolate-and-confectionery.p: Chocolate as a drink is Mesoamerica’s gift: on Mexico’s Pacific coast people were drinking it, bitter and frothy, by 1900 BC. The chocolatier’s craft came much later, and in Europe. In Vevey in 1875 Daniel Peter, helped by Henri Nestlé, brought milk chocolate to market. In Bern in 1879 Rodolphe Lindt invented the conche, which warms and stirs chocolate for days until the grit is gone. Then in Brussels in 1912 Jean Neuhaus II made the first filled chocolate bonbons, the pralines. Today the craft is most alive in Belgium, which in 2012 counted 500 chocolatiers and 2,000 chocolate shops, one for every 5,500 people, and where Antwerp hosts the 2026 World Chocolate Masters final, the first ever held outside Paris.

japanese-knife-making.p: Japan’s great knife towns grew out of tobacco and lost swords. The Portuguese brought tobacco to Japan in the mid-sixteenth century, and in the latter half of that century the smiths of Sakai began forging small knives to cut the leaf. The Tokugawa shogunate later granted their blades an official mark of quality. In the mid-Edo period the deba appeared, and many other cooks’ knives followed. Then on 28 March 1876 the Haitōrei edict banned most people from carrying swords in public, and many swordsmiths turned to kitchen cutlery to survive. Today the craft is most alive in Sakai, whose forged blades, Japan’s crafts association says, are most of the knives Japanese professional chefs use, and in Tosa, where a land survey of 1590 already counted 399 blacksmiths and the forges still work.

sources.what: Japan traditional crafts association (kougeihin.jp), Sakai Uchihamono
Search summary of Sakai International Promotion Council and others (corroborating late-16th-century tobacco knives)

thai-massage.p: Thai healers honour Jīvaka, remembered in Buddhist scripture as the Buddha’s physician, but that is devotion, not a documented birth. The record begins at the court of Ayutthaya, where law from the reign of King Borommatrailokkanat, 1448 to 1488, names a high-ranking Department of Massage Physicians. Then in the 1830s, as King Rama III restored Wat Pho in Bangkok, some fifty court scholars carved the temple’s medical knowledge in stone, including sixty plaques mapping the body’s pressure points. Today the craft is most alive in Bangkok. Wat Pho opened Thailand’s first ministry-approved school of Thai medicine in 1955, its pavilions are still massage classrooms, and in 2019 UNESCO inscribed Nuad Thai as heritage of humanity.

sources.what: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Nuad Thai

kitesurfing.p: Kitesurfing was born in Brittany. On 16 November 1984 Bruno and Dominique Legaignoux, brothers from Quimper, filed a patent for an inflatable-framed propulsive wing: a kite with an air-filled leading edge that floats when it falls into the sea. In the United States Cory Roeseler was chasing the same idea, and his KiteSki went on sale in 1994. In 1996 Manu Bertin and Laird Hamilton showed the new sport off the coast of Maui, and the first competition was held there in September 1998. Today it is most alive on Brazil’s Ceará coast, where the 2025 GKA freestyle world titles were decided at Taíba, the women’s won by the Brazilian Bruna Kajiya, and where the tour’s 2026 final was set for October.

sources.what: Diário do Nordeste, GKA 2026 freestyle final at Ilha do Guajiru
GKA Kite World Tour, 2026 season announcement

photography.p: The first photograph was made in France. Between June and July 1827, at his estate of Le Gras in Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, Nicéphore Niépce fixed the view from an upper window on a plate coated with bitumen. It is the oldest surviving photograph made with a camera. In 1829 he went into partnership with Louis Daguerre, and on 19 August 1839 Daguerre’s process was presented to the academies in Paris and given by the French state free to the world, except in Britain, where Daguerre had patented it. In England that same year Henry Fox Talbot showed his paper photographs, and in 1841 his calotype brought the negative from which many prints can be made. Today the craft is most alive in Arles, whose Rencontres, founded in 1970, drew a record 175,000 visitors in 2025.

sources.what: Wikipedia, View from the Window at Le Gras
L'Œil de la Photographie, Arles 2025: Disobedient Images
Phototrend on the Rencontres d’Arles (175,000 visitors in 2025)

modernist-spanish-cuisine.p: This cuisine’s most famous kitchen stood in a cove. ElBulli stood above Cala Montjoi, near Roses on the Costa Brava. Ferran Adrià joined its kitchen in 1984 and took full charge in 1987, and from there came the foams and the spherification it made famous. Restaurant magazine’s list named it the best restaurant in the world five times, in 2002 and every year from 2006 to 2009. It served its last meals in 2011, closing on 30 July, and became a foundation for creative cooking. Its cooks carried the work on. Today the craft is most alive in Barcelona, where three of them, Oriol Castro, Eduard Xatruch and Mateu Casañas, opened Disfrutar in December 2014; in 2024 it was named the world’s best restaurant.

sources.what: Restaurant Online (William Reed, publisher of the 50 Best), 6 June 2024

yacht-crew-and-stcw.p: This trade has no single birthplace, but its rulebook has a birthday. On 7 July 1978 governments meeting at what is now the International Maritime Organization adopted the STCW Convention, the first to set basic requirements for the training, certification and watchkeeping of seafarers on an international level. It came into force on 28 April 1984, was overhauled in 1995 and brought up to date at Manila in 2010. Its basic training has four parts: personal survival techniques, fire prevention and firefighting, elementary first aid, and personal safety and social responsibilities. Today one of the trade’s busiest hubs is Antibes, home of the Professional Yachting Association, run by yachting professionals since 1991, which gave its membership as 11,518 at the start of 2026.

sources.what: IMO, International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers (STCW)
US Code of Federal Regulations, 46 CFR 11.302 (basic training under STCW)

self-sufficiency.p: Keeping food through the winter is older than any book, but the craft of sealing it safely has a birthplace. Nicolas Appert began experimenting in 1795, and in 1804 his works at Massy, near Paris, became the world’s first food-bottling factory. In 1810 the French state paid him 12,000 francs and he published The Art of Preserving Animal and Vegetable Substances. The modern case for growing all of it yourself was made from a smallholding near Orford in Suffolk, where John Seymour wrote The Fat of the Land in 1961, then The Complete Book of Self-Sufficiency in 1976. Today it is lived daily at Sunseed, in the village of Los Molinos in Almería: a solar-powered, food-growing project that turns forty in 2026.

cold-exposure-wim-hof-method.p: This craft is young, and it has one author. Wim Hof was born in Sittard, in the Netherlands, in 1959; at seventeen he felt a sudden urge to jump into the freezing water of a park canal, and his routine of breathing and ice grew from there. In 2014 doctors at Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen published a trial: twelve volunteers trained for ten days in his breathing, meditation and ice-water immersion produced far more adrenaline and had fewer flu-like symptoms after a dose of bacterial toxin. The breathing is never done in water, because practitioners have drowned. The method is most alive in Przesieka, in Poland’s Karkonosze mountains, at the guesthouse where, the Wim Hof Method says, all its teacher trainings have been held.

sources.what: Kox et al., PNAS 2014, abstract via Europe PMC (PMID 24799686)
Wim Hof Method official activities page, Travel Przesieka

windsurfing-and-wing-foil.p: The sailboard has two American beginnings. In 1964 Newman Darby of Pennsylvania built a rudderless board with a pivoting sail. The version that spread came from Santa Monica, California, where Jim Drake and Hoyle Schweitzer founded Windsurfing International in 1968 and were granted a joint patent for the rig in 1970; by 1984 it was an Olympic sport. The wing is newer. Tony Logosz of Slingshot tested his first wing prototypes in the Columbia Gorge in 2011, Flash Austin tried handheld wings on foils in Maui in 2018, and by 2019 they were on sale. Maui is where windsurfing is most alive today, and where the wing was first tried on a foil. At Ho’okipa the Aloha Classic closes the world wave tour each autumn; in 2025, its 41st edition, Marc Paré left as world champion for the first time.

jewelry-and-goldsmithing.p: People were hammering gold into ornaments long before anyone wrote. Near Varna, on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, a cemetery dated to about 4500 BC held some three thousand gold objects, the oldest gold jewellery yet found. Renaissance Florence made the goldsmith’s bench a school for artists: Filippo Brunelleschi was apprenticed as a goldsmith at fifteen and became a master in 1398. In 1593 Grand Duke Ferdinando I cleared the butchers and fishmongers off the Ponte Vecchio and forbade any trade on it but precious metals. Florence is where that bench is still most visibly alive: the bridge is home only to small jewellers, and through some workshop windows you can still watch goldsmiths making pieces by hand.

sources.what: Italia.it (Italian national tourism board), Florentine jewellery on the Ponte Vecchio

sushi-and-washoku.p: Sushi began as a way to keep fish, not to serve it: fish packed in rice to preserve it, first in Southeast Asia, possibly in the Mekong basin, long before it reached Japan. The craft a sushi chef practises was born in Edo, today’s Tokyo. Hanaya Yohei is believed to have invented nigiri, the hand-pressed form, around 1824, and edomae, fish from Edo Bay, is still a by-word for sushi done properly. In 2013 UNESCO inscribed washoku, the wider Japanese food culture, on its list of intangible heritage. Tokyo is where the craft is most alive today. In October 2018 the city moved its fish trade from Tsukiji to Toyosu, which opened as the largest wholesale fish market in the world.

organic-farm-to-table-cooking.p: Cooking from the field outside the door took shape as a deliberate craft in two kitchens. In 1964 Myrtle Allen opened a restaurant in the dining room of Ballymaloe House in East Cork, changing her menu every day with what was in season. In 1971 Alice Waters opened Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California, building direct ties with local growers, and it became one of the places the farm-to-table movement started. Ballymaloe is where the craft is still most alive as a school. Darina Allen and her brother Rory O’Connell started the Ballymaloe Cookery School in 1983 at Kinoith, about four kilometres from the house, and it still teaches inside its own 100-acre organic farm.

hatha-and-vinyasa-yoga.p: Haṭha yoga was written down long before it reached a studio. Its earliest substantial text, the Amṛtasiddhi, dates from around the eleventh century, and in the fifteenth Svātmārāma gathered the older teachings into the Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā. The flow came later, and in Mysore. Engaged by Maharaja Krishna Raja Wadiyar IV in 1926, Tirumalai Krishnamacharya opened a yoga school in the Jaganmohan Palace in 1933 and is widely credited with joining breath to movement; two of his students, K. Pattabhi Jois and B. K. S. Iyengar, went on to found Ashtanga vinyasa yoga and Iyengar Yoga. Today the practice is most alive in Rishikesh, where Parmarth Niketan, on the bank of the Ganges, expected nearly 1,200 people from nearly 80 nations at its International Yoga Festival in March 2026.

freediving.p: Long before it was a sport, sponge divers rode a stone weight, the skandalopetra, as deep as thirty metres on one breath. The sport of going deep was born in Italy. In 1949, off Capri, Raimondo Bucher descended to 29 metres before a commission, and in 1950, answering a challenge from the Neapolitan Underwater Club, he reached 30 metres, the first official freediving world record. Enzo Maiorca of Syracuse reached 50 metres in 1961, and his rivalry with Jacques Mayol inspired the film The Big Blue. Today the sport’s deepest divers still gather each July at Dean’s Blue Hole in the Bahamas, 202 metres deep, for William Trubridge’s Vertical Blue, where in 2025 Alenka Artnik equalled the deepest dive ever made by a woman, 123 metres on a monofin.

sources.what: DIVERNET, 'Freedivers Jerald & Artnik worldbeaters in Bahamas'

rock-climbing.p: Rock climbing as a sport was born in Europe in the second half of the nineteenth century. In 1864 gymnasts from Bad Schandau climbed the Falkenstein in Saxon Switzerland, and in June 1886 Walter Parry Haskett Smith climbed Napes Needle in the Lake District, the ascent widely taken as the start of the sport in Britain. The big-wall craft grew up later, in Yosemite. Warren Harding’s team finished the Nose of El Capitan in 1958, after some 47 days of climbing spread over two seasons, and Lynn Hill climbed it free in 1993. That granite is still where the limits move. In January 2015 Tommy Caldwell and Kevin Jorgeson freed the Dawn Wall after 19 days, and on 3 June 2017 Alex Honnold climbed Freerider alone and without a rope, in 3 hours and 56 minutes.

perfumery.p: One of the oldest perfumers known by name is a woman. Around 1200 BC a cuneiform tablet from Assur records Tapputi, head of the palace perfumers, distilling flowers, myrrh and balsam with oil and water. The perfumer’s craft as Europe knows it grew up in Grasse, in Provence, a town of tanners. Since at least the sixteenth century its people have grown and processed perfume plants and composed fragrant blends, and in 1614 the king recognised its new guild of glovers-perfumers. It is still most alive there. In 2018 UNESCO inscribed the perfume skills of the Pays de Grasse, from the field to the art of composition, and about sixty companies in and around the town employ 3,500 people.

wine-and-sommellerie.p: The word is French. In Middle French a sommelier was the court official in charge of moving supplies, and the name probably goes back to the driver of a pack animal. The examined craft, naming a wine by its taste and proving it before examiners, was born in Britain: the first Master of Wine examinations were held in 1953, and the first Master Sommelier examination followed in 1969. London is still where its examiners are based. The Institute of Masters of Wine works from there, and since that first exam only some five hundred people have earned the title. In Bermondsey, the Wine & Spirit Education Trust, founded in 1969, saw 134,000 candidates take its qualifications in 2023/24.

Institute of Masters of Wine, About us

wildlife-photography.p: Among the first to make a craft of wildlife photography were two farmers’ sons from Thwaite, in Yorkshire’s Swaledale. In 1892 Cherry Kearton made the first photograph ever taken of a bird’s nest with eggs, and with his brother Richard he learned that the camera had to disappear: they worked from inside a hollow ox in 1900 and a stuffed sheep in 1901. The hide is still the heart of the craft, and its modern form was born at the edge of Pusztaszer, in Hungary, by the wetlands. There, in the spring of 2005, Bence Máté began photographing from behind one-way glass, so shy animals are not disturbed. He is the only photographer to have won the Wildlife Photographer of the Year grand prize as both a young and an adult entrant.

ashtanga-yoga.p: Ashtanga yoga was born in Mysore, in southern India. On 11 August 1933 Tirumalai Krishnamacharya opened a yoga school in a wing of the city’s Jaganmohan Palace, and among his students was K. Pattabhi Jois, who had first met him at twelve. Krishnamacharya said the sequences came from an old text, the Yoga Korunta, later eaten by ants; that is legend, and Jois’s own son said Krishnamacharya created them. Jois opened his institute in Mysore in 1948. After the Belgian André Van Lysebeth trained with him in 1964 and printed his address in a book, Westerners began to come, and they still do. For the 2026 season at Sharath Yoga Centre, the family’s shala on the edge of Mysore, demand was such that places were allotted at random.

spearfishing.p: People have speared fish since the Palaeolithic, but the sport of hunting on one breath took off in the 1920s on the Mediterranean coast of France and Italy, by swimmers wearing only watertight goggles. It helped bring in the modern diving mask, fins and snorkel; the Frenchman Louis de Corlieu, who had shown a first prototype to naval officers in 1914, patented his swimfins in April 1933. In Antibes, the American writer Guy Gilpatric hunted the same water and in 1938 published The Compleat Goggler, held to be the first full guide to the sport; he drew Jacques-Yves Cousteau and Hans Hass into it. Today the craft is most alive where its champions come from: at the 2025 World Championship in Brazil, Tahiti’s Dell Lamartinière and Taina Orth won both individual titles, and Spain took the men’s team gold.

ski-touring-and-splitboard.p: The oldest skis yet found, in northern Russia, are some eight thousand years old, and in 1555 Olaus Magnus described the skis of the Sámi, one of them lined with animal skin for grip. Touring as a mountain craft grew up later, in the Alps. In 1911 skiers first completed the Haute Route, the high-hut route between Chamonix and Zermatt. The splitboard that caught on came from Utah: in 1991 Brett Kobernik took a crude prototype to Voilé, a Salt Lake City ski maker, and in 1994 they began selling it. The Alps are still where the craft is most alive: in February 2026 ski mountaineering, touring’s racing form, made its Olympic debut at Bormio, in Italy.

SLUG Magazine, Voilé and the Splitboard

french-pastry-and-patisserie.p: French pâtisserie as an exacting trade took its shape in Paris. In 1798 Marie-Antoine Carême, a Parisian boy, began his apprenticeship at Sylvain Bailly’s pâtisserie on the rue Vivienne. He built sugar centrepieces modelled on temples and pyramids, built croquembouches and refined the vol-au-vent, and in 1815 published Le Pâtissier royal parisien. In France the maître pâtissier is still a title earned through apprenticeship and a written exam. Today the craft is most alive in Japan as much as in France. At the World Pastry Cup, held every two years in Lyon since 1989, France has won eight golds, but Japan won in 2023 and again in 2025, when Masanori Hata, Yuji Matoba and Ryu Miyazaki beat France into second.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Coupe du Monde de la Pâtisserie

modern-new-technique-cuisine.p: Count Rumford described cooking at low heat in 1799, but the modern kitchen toolkit came into the restaurant in France and Catalonia. In 1974, at the Troisgros restaurant in Roanne, the chef Georges Pralus cooked foie gras under vacuum and found it kept its shape, its fat and a better texture: sous-vide had reached the restaurant kitchen. In 1988 the physicist Nicholas Kurti and the chemist Hervé This named the science behind such work ‘molecular and physical gastronomy’. Then on the Costa Brava, Ferran and Albert Adrià’s team at elBulli brought alginate spheres into the restaurant, and their Texturas line sold gums such as xanthan to chefs. Today the craft is most alive in Catalonia. In Barcelona, Disfrutar, opened in 2014 by three chefs who met at elBulli, was named the best restaurant in the world in 2024.

vipassana-and-meditation.p: The word comes from the Pali texts of early Buddhism, where a meditator is told to sit beneath a tree and simply watch the breath. But the ten-day course taught today was shaped in Burma. There, meditation practice was revived in the 1700s by the monk Medawi, and Ledi Sayadaw (1846–1923) opened it to lay people as well as monks. The lay teacher Sayagyi U Ba Khin trained S. N. Goenka for fourteen years, and in 1969 Goenka began teaching in India. Today the craft is most alive at Dhamma Giri in Igatpuri, which held its first ten-day course in October 1976 and now seats around 600 students in each one, at the head of a tradition now taught at hundreds of centres around the world.

sailing-and-yachtmaster.p: The word yacht is Dutch: a jacht was a light, fast sailing vessel of the Dutch Republic. When Charles II was restored to the English throne in 1660 he was given one, and the first recorded yacht race followed in 1661. The skipper’s ticket came later. In 1938, at the Admiralty’s request, Britain’s Board of Trade began examining Yachtmasters, and in 1973 the Royal Yachting Association issued its first certificate. Today the craft is most alive on the Solent. The RYA has run the scheme from Hamble since 2003, and Cowes Week, first raced in 1826, still puts some 450 boats on the start line. By its fiftieth year, 336 centres in 37 countries taught it, and just over half of those examined each year were not British.

safari-and-wildlife-guiding.p: Guiding people on foot through wild country, to watch animals rather than shoot them, has one of its first grounds in South Africa. By 1958 half of South Africa’s iMfolozi Game Reserve was proclaimed a wilderness area, among the first official wilderness areas in Africa. In 1959 Ian Player and the game tracker Magqubu Ntombela led the first official Natal Parks Board trail into it, and the trails they began are still walked today. Today the craft is most alive in South Africa, where the Field Guides Association of Southern Africa, founded in 1990 and based in Hoedspruit, sets the standards guides train and are assessed against. In 2024 it helped found a sister association for East Africa, built on those same standards.

italian-cuisine-and-pasta.p: Nobody can name the first plate of pasta, and the old story that Marco Polo brought it from China is a myth. One of the earliest firm records on Italian soil comes from 1154, when the geographer al-Idrisi described buildings at Trabia, in Sicily, making vast quantities of itriyya, strands of dough dried before cooking and shipped everywhere. One Italian table came later. In 1891 Pellegrino Artusi of Forlimpopoli, unable to find a publisher, paid to print his own book of recipes gathered from across the regions. Today Bologna guards the craft most closely: its Chamber of Commerce has kept a gold sample of the cooked tagliatella, eight millimetres wide, since 1972, and in a country whose cooking UNESCO added to the intangible heritage of humanity in 2025.

lymphatic-drainage.p: Manual lymphatic drainage has two named inventors. In the early 1930s the Danish doctors Emil and Estrid Vodder were working on the French Riviera with patients who had chronic colds and enlarged lymph nodes. In 1932 they began to study the lymph system and to develop gentle hand techniques to move lymph, and in 1936 they showed the method in Paris. It took deep root in the German-speaking world. In Walchsee, in the Tyrol, Günther and Hildegard Wittlinger worked with Emil Vodder to bring it to Austria more than fifty years ago, and their academy and clinic still teach and treat there. Across the border, Germany’s statutory health insurance pays for it, and since October 2024 a doctor treating staged lymphoedema can leave the physiotherapist to set the length of each session.

sound-healing.p: Sound as a path inward is old. The Nadabindu Upanishad, a Sanskrit yoga text some scholars date to around the start of the Common Era, tells the yogi to listen for an inner sound, first like the ocean or thunder, then finer, to a single note. The singing bowl is younger than its story. Scholars find no credible record of Tibetans playing bowls this way; the first written mention is a 1972 album, Tibetan Bells, by the American musicians Henry Wolff and Nancy Hennings. Sound healing as a profession grew up in the West after that. The British Academy of Sound Therapy, which says it was Britain’s first, opened in 2000, and the Globe Institute in Sausalito, California, calls itself the only state-approved college of sound healing in the United States.

surfing.p: Surfing was born among the Polynesians, and in Hawaii it ran deep through life, faith and rank. Hawaiians called it heʻe nalu, wave sliding. The first European account comes from Captain Cook’s 1769 voyage, when Joseph Banks watched Tahitians ride the surf on the stern of an old canoe. In the summer of 1914–15 the Hawaiian Olympic swimming champion Duke Kahanamoku rode a board at Freshwater and Manly in Sydney, and the craft took root on another continent. Today Hawaii still crowns the season: the World Surf League’s Championship Tour ends each December with the Pipe Masters on Oahu’s North Shore. In Europe the tour stops at Supertubos in Peniche, Portugal, and Ericeira, just down the coast, became Europe’s first World Surfing Reserve in 2011.

pottery-and-ceramics.p: The oldest pots anyone has found come from Xianrendong Cave in Jiangxi, southern China. Hunter-gatherers fired them about 20,000 years ago and cooked in them, perhaps boiling clams and snails, some ten thousand years before farming reached the region. The wheel came far later; many scholars credit the Sumerians of Mesopotamia, and a stone potter’s wheel from Ur is dated to about 3129 BC. The same province is where the craft is most alive today. Jingdezhen made porcelain from the Song dynasty to the Qing, and its imperial kilns served the court. In July 2026 its handicraft porcelain sites became the first World Heritage site themed on porcelain, and the city counts more than 60,000 jingpiao, makers who moved there, thousands of them from more than 60 countries.

new-basque-cuisine.p: Basque cooks have always worked from the market and the grill, but the new Basque kitchen has a birth year. In 1976 a young Juan Mari Arzak sat at a gastronomy round table in Madrid, where Paul Bocuse said the key was market cooking. Two months later Arzak and Pedro Subijana were in Bocuse’s kitchen in Lyon, learning nouvelle cuisine at the stove. That December, back home, the group held its first meeting at the Jaizubia restaurant in Hondarribia, and Nueva Cocina Vasca had begun. It is still most alive around San Sebastián. In the 2026 Michelin Guide, three of Spain’s sixteen three-star restaurants stand there: Arzak, Subijana’s Akelaŕe on Mount Igeldo, and Martín Berasategui in nearby Lasarte-Oria.

lifestyle-medicine.p: Lifestyle medicine has no ancient birthplace. The idea that daily habits shape health is as old as Hippocrates, but the name and the institutions are American and recent. In 1991 Ernst Wynder of the American Health Foundation in New York, who had spoken out against cigarettes since 1950, titled a paper “Listen to nature: the challenge of lifestyle medicine”. James Rippe published a textbook called Lifestyle Medicine in 1999, and the American College of Lifestyle Medicine held its first general meeting in 2004. The United States is still its centre. Its board began certifying in 2017 with 221 US physicians, and by 2022 counted 2,445 diplomates.

_learnLines_comment: The immersive line under the place name on every craft page's place card, keyed by DESTINATION id. Hand-written, for the same reason craftFamilies is hand-grouped: every attempt to compose one from the craft blurb plus the destination's `why` read as a machine talking. And compressing a researched sentence is exactly where a claim quietly changes — 'the most photographed big-cat ground on earth' is NOT 'where the most big cats are', and only one of those is true. RULE: a line here may say nothing its own `why` does not already say. Where a destination is a heritage source with no vouched school, or is an experts-only spot, the line must NOT begin 'Learn to' — it would promise teaching that is not there. A missing line is fine: the card simply shows none. See LEARN_LINES in build-atlas-pages.py.

_sayLines_comment: The FIRST line a card says, keyed by DESTINATION id. Where learnLines is the researched sentence, this is the card's own title: 'Learn to photograph big cats from a camp' with 'in Kenya' on the line under it. At rest a card names the craft — 'Learn Wildlife Photography in Pusztaszer, Hungary' — and while it walks its places this replaces the craft's name with what you would actually be doing in THAT one. Write it against the destination's WHOLE record, not just its `why`: schoolsInfo carries the course and the school's own blurb, which is where 'one-way glass', 'on the Russian border' and 'four to a group' come from. Three rules. It may say nothing that record does not already say (gated by learn_line_drift). Where there is no vouched school it must not begin 'Learn to' — that would promise teaching that is not there. And it never carries the place: the card prints the place on the next line and would say it twice. Length is free — the card reserves the height of the longest line it can ever show — but short is the point of the line. A missing line is fine: the card keeps naming the craft. See SAY_LINES in build-atlas-pages.py.

_craftImages_comment: A licensed picture OF THE CRAFT, for a craft no school has photographed. Keyed by craft id, but TAKEN AT ONE PLACE: Arnaud, 27 September 2026, 'make sure the photo on the skill card of the Atlas matches the location of the card'. It used to say the picture belonged nowhere and could ride any card, and 16 of 22 were of somewhere else (yoga in Bali under Mysore, a Namibian farm under Greater Kruger, a Californian surfer under Waikiki). Every entry ships six things: src, alt, credit, licence, sourceUrl and takenAt, the destination id the picture was taken at (plus an optional focal). The build refuses one whose takenAt is not the place the card rests on, and the browse page drops it when a filter moves the card to another town. takenAt is only as good as the Commons page: read the description, categories or coordinates, never the title alone. A licence with no source is not checkable, and being checkable is this map's whole claim. THE TWO CLASSES MAY NEVER BE CONFUSED: a craft image is drawn by .craftshot/--illus, never .cardshot/--shot; its credit names its maker and its LICENCE and stops, and may never start with 'Photo:', which is reserved for a picture a school sent us; and the build REFUSES a craft image on a craft that already has a school photograph, because the school's own room always wins. IT MUST BE A PICTURE OF THE CRAFT, NEVER OF A PLACE — a spherified pearl is what modernist technique looks like anywhere; a school's front door under another town's name is the same lie as composing a place sentence. AND NO IMAGE IS BETTER THAN A GENERIC ONE: a craft with no truthful picture keeps the typographic card, and that is a finished state, not a gap to fill with stock. Lifestyle Medicine is the case that proves it — its own sheet says it is a credential, not a place. 10 crafts carry one after the 27 September re-hunt (8 replaced, sushi and ski touring kept). Modernist Spanish Cuisine lost its licensed picture the same day to the photographs Vakuum sent us: a school's own room comes first. Eleven lost theirs because Commons holds nothing honest taken at the card's place: ashtanga-yoga (Mysore), cold-exposure-wim-hof-method (Karkonosze), jewelry-and-goldsmithing (Florence: shop windows only), organic-farm-to-table-cooking (Ballymaloe: empty gardens), pottery-and-ceramics (Mashiko: kilns, no potter), sound-healing (Nepal: bowls on market stalls), spearfishing (Cote d'Azur), vipassana-and-meditation (Dhamma Giri: the pagoda only, a landmark), wildlife-photography (Pusztaszer), windsurfing-and-wing-foil (Karpathos), yacht-crew-and-stcw (Antibes: yacht portraits, no crew). A school's photograph, or a Flickr CC BY find, is the way back for each. FIVE ARE DELIBERATELY EMPTY and should stay that way until something honest exists: japanese-knife-making (Commons holds museum record shots of finished blades and European smiths at European forges — a German smith under the word Shimanto is the lie this class guards against), perfumery (liquor distilling, 18th-century engravings and a petroleum refinery; no perfumer at the organ exists free), lymphatic-drainage (generic massage, none of it the clinical technique), new-basque-cuisine (finished plates and bar pintxos, nothing of the Arzak/Subijana movement — and pintxos would blur the very distinction the Atlas just drew), and lifestyle-medicine (never searched: its own sheet says it is a credential, not a place). self-sufficiency was searched and left empty too — a pool of six, none of it honest. See CRAFT_IMAGES in scripts/build-atlas-pages.py.

_schoolShotDebt_comment: What the Atlas owes here is a picture from the SCHOOL — the room a reader would be standing in, sent by the people who teach in it. 88 outreach letters have produced five. So this counts open crafts with NO school photograph, and a licensed craft image does not pay it off: a stranger's frame of the craft makes a card legible, it is not a school opening its door. Count a stand-in as paid and the ratchet congratulates us for buying stock. _measure_comment: The Measure — the per-craft answer to the promise the trust block already makes: what we check before we send you anywhere. Five questions on the five dots, asked in the same words and the same order on every craft, because a legend a reader has to relearn is not a legend (the build refuses any other wording — see MEASURE_QUESTIONS in scripts/atlas_hub.py). The instrument's own shorthand — the room, the door, the bench, the ground, the stretch — stays in THE-MEASURE-META-PROMPT.md and never reaches a reader: on the page we ask the question rather than name it. Rendered only for crafts listed here; a craft with no entry shows no meter, which is an absence and not a zero. Desk research stops at three — whether a craft is alive in its place, and whether there is enough there to keep you going, are exactly what a brochure claims, and only somebody standing in the room settles them. Never write a line that ranks one craft against another, and never borrow a restaurant guide's award language: we report what we found and hand the reader the decision.

modernist-spanish-cuisine.verdict: If this craft already pulls you, there is enough here to go on — we have not stood in it, so we will not tell you to cross the world for it yet

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Le Cordon Bleu Madrid — the school this craft recommends, and so the one that has to answer — names the chefs who teach its Spanish Cuisine programmes on its own Meet the Chefs page, read 17 September 2026: Natalia Vázquez at their head, with chef instructors David Vela, Manuel Lucas and Diego Muñoz, one of them described there as joining the teaching team for the Spanish Cooking Diploma in 2016. Barcelona answers it a second way: Martín Lippo teaches modernist technique himself, in his own laboratory.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: You can book your way in, on dates. Madrid's avant-garde teaching is the last third of a nine-month Spanish Cuisine Diploma, and their own syllabus names the block — spherifications, low-temperature cooking, the fundamentals of molecular cuisine. Barcelona's lab courses are shorter. The stage is the other road and it is a real one, but it is applied for with a CV and nobody can promise you one: only one of the two is a way in you can book. Your hands can ruin the work on either.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: The strongest thing this craft has — and the community dots above are the evidence for it, not a second opinion. Barcelona is where the elBulli cooks actually landed, and Disfrutar, opened by three of them, was named the world's best restaurant in 2024. Madrid gathers the whole avant-garde once a year at Madrid Fusión, running since 2003 and reaching its 25th edition in February 2027. There is a generation above you here, and one below.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and this is the question that separates this craft from the travelling toolkit. Madrid Fusión — Alimentos de España — has been the vanguard's own congress since 2003, and it happens here rather than in any of the places the technique has since reached. That technique goes anywhere; this cuisine came from here and still argues with itself in the same rooms.

evidence.what: Madrid Fusión — Alimentos de España

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been, and there is more here than an attendance certificate: the Superior Certificate is a real nine-month qualification, and a stage in a kitchen of this lineage is months on the line. As high as this craft goes is very high — three Michelin stars at DiverXO, the world's best restaurant list at Disfrutar.

lifestyle-medicine.verdict: A real medical board certification and not a travel destination — closed to anyone without a clinical degree, and listed here against a whole country rather than a place

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Yes, in the institution-taught form. The American Board of Lifestyle Medicine is a certifying board and the American College of Lifestyle Medicine is the body that trains toward it; the credential belongs to them rather than to a teacher. lymphatic-drainage.verdict: One village, one academy, one method — the training is as serious as anything on this map, and the place has nothing to do with why

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Yes, in the form this craft actually takes. Nobody apprentices under a named master here: manual lymph drainage is transmitted by a body with a lineage, and both are named — the Dr. Vodder Academy, carrying Emil Vodder's method through the Wittlinger family since the early 1970s, teaching beside their own working lymphoedema clinic. We name no individual instructor because the credential is the academy's, not a person's, and that is the shape of the craft rather than a gap in the research.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?

A hundred and eighty hours across two two-week blocks, taught in German, the next starting 9 November 2026 (academy course page, read 5 October 2026). conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: No — and this is the honest answer rather than a criticism. The test is whether this craft, taught this way, would make sense anywhere else, and it plainly would: the Vodder certificate is taught by recognised schools in several countries and the method does not change with the ground. Walchsee is where the academy is. It is not where the craft lives.

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?

conditions.t: Yes in three of the four places, each a named living person teaching in their own lab: Martin Lippo at Vakuum in Barcelona, Éric Briffard at Le Cordon Bleu Paris, Miguel Ángel Cepeda in Puebla and Mexico City. Three out of four is still more than anything else on this map manages. The fourth has changed shape rather than closed: Sous Vide Australia's site now offers bespoke training built for a venue's own team, not the public workshops this map listed, and its card says so. ⛔ Where we stand: EducatedTraveler runs a paid week with Martin Lippo, so we are not a neutral party about him. Nobody pays to be on this map and no money reaches us from him; the way in without us is his own site, martinlippo.com.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open, and unusually so for the avant-garde. Melbourne is no longer one of them: what is offered there is training a venue books for its own team. And the hands can ruin it — a spherification bath and liquid nitrogen are unforgiving, which is why the labs are labs.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?

Sous-vide was worked out at Troisgros in 1974 and now belongs to every kitchen with a circulator. Catalonia's claim on the avant-garde is real and it is graded on this map's modernist Spanish cuisine page, where the restaurants are. Here you are buying a technique, and the technique is portable by design.

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been, and this craft has no ladder to point at instead: its own record says there is no single formal body and that the qualification is a certificate of attendance. That is not a criticism of the labs, which are teaching real skills. It does mean that what happens after the course is entirely up to you and your own kitchen.

pottery-and-ceramics.verdict: Four towns where clay is the local industry rather than the local attraction — and not one living potter named among them, which is our gap and a morning's work to close

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Empty in all four places, and one of them worse than empty. Mashiko's entry named Tatsuzo Shimaoka until today — a Living National Treasure who died on 11 December 2007, now moved to where the craft comes from, which is where he belonged; Jingdezhen, the Six Ancient Kilns and St Ives name nobody at all. A craft taught hand over hand at a wheel is a craft where the person is the whole thing, so this is the first question to fix on this page and the cheapest — every one of these studios has a potter whose name is on their own website.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Wide open, at every length. Half-day and full-day wheel classes in Mashiko with live-in stays, hands-on sessions at Seto and Tokoname, one-to-six-month residencies at Sanbao and the Pottery Workshop in Jingdezhen, and the year-long Leach Year in St Ives. And clay is the plainest case on this map of hands that can ruin it: a wall pulled wrong collapses, and a pot can still die in the kiln after a week of work.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, and at both ends. Jingdezhen is the densest working cohort of ceramicists anywhere, with Sanbao hosting dozens of makers a year alongside the university's international work camps. Mashiko carries about 250 potteries in one town. In residencies of that shape there is always somebody further on than you at the next wheel, and somebody behind you.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and Mashiko settles it in the town's own words rather than a school's. The Mashiko Tourist Association calls pottery the town's main industry, counts around 250 potteries and about 50 ceramic shops, and has run a Pottery Fair twice a year since 1966 — roughly 50 shops and as many as 800 tents, drawing about 600,000 people, with the 2026 autumn fair set for 31 October to 3 November. That is a town earning its living from the craft, not a school renting a room in one.

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. Only somebody who stayed past the introductory course can say what is above it.

rock-climbing.verdict: Four of the best-known crags on earth, taught by certified guides nobody has named for you — the standard is the point of the craft, and the person is still the thing you are buying

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Empty at four of the five places, and largely by design. Rock climbing is taught by guides an outside body certifies — AMGA in the United States, the IFMGA internationally, the state diploma through ENSA in Chamonix — so instructors are interchangeable on purpose and no school advertises one. Kalymnos is the exception, and it is the place added last: Joe Fratianni, an Austrian state-certified instructor and an AMGA guide working toward IFMGA, and Simon Montmory, whose courses are named for the grade they take you to. Two names on one island do not answer the question for Yosemite, Chamonix, the Peak or Joshua Tree — at those four, ask who your guide will be and what they are certified to lead. Chamonix's entry named the Compagnie des Guides, founded in 1821, which is a company rather than a person; it has been moved to where the craft comes from.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open and properly laddered. Yosemite runs sequential multi-day classes from 'Welcome to the Rock' to a two-day big wall course, capped at six students an instructor. Chamonix's two-day multi-pitch course asks for French grade IV before you book it, which is a door with a standard on it. Plas y Brenin runs a five-day residential. And the hands can ruin it: you place your own protection and you build your own anchors, which is the whole of why the instruction exists.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, and the ladder runs both ways. Joshua Tree carries a dense winter cohort and is where the AMGA Single Pitch Instructor course is taught, so the people beside you include those learning to teach. Sheffield's walls hold the Peak's climbers between crag days, Yosemite Valley has thousands passing through every season, and Kalymnos fills each spring and autumn around an international festival every October — the same thing on a season's rhythm.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and the United States National Park Service says so about Yosemite without selling anything: it calls the Valley one of the world's greatest climbing areas, requires a wilderness climbing permit from everybody sleeping on a big wall, and manages the peregrine falcon closures around the routes. A park authority building its permit system around climbers is a place organised by the craft. Kalymnos says it a second way: the island's guidebook counts 4,216 bolted sport routes and keeps a public log of the volunteers who re-bolt them, which is a community maintaining its own crags rather than a school renting them.

conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. The ladder here is unusually legible — single pitch, multi-pitch, aid, the AMGA and IFMGA guide certifications above all of it — and El Capitan is about as clear a thing to set out to do as any craft on this map offers. What a season on the ground is actually like, and whether the people stay, is not on any page.

safari-and-wildlife-guiding.verdict: The longest courses on this map, on ground owned by the people who live on it — and the school we send you to does name the people who teach them

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: EcoTraining — the school this craft recommends, and so the one that has to answer — names its instructors on its own Meet the Team page, twelve of them, read 17 September 2026. Nature Guide Training names Lee Gutteridge, its owner and trainer. African Guide Academy names four trainers in the Okavango. Two rooms still name nobody: Bhejane in Zululand and the Koiyaki Guiding School, which trains young Maasai in their own conservancy. In a craft where you learn to walk up on dangerous game, who is carrying the rifle beside you is not a detail — ask for the name and the trails-guide qualification of whoever leads your walks.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open, and long. Fifty-five and sixty-day residential courses in the Greater Kruger and at Mashatu, a one-year professional programme in KwaZulu-Natal, a one-year Maasai guiding course in Naboisho. Published, bookable, and with the FGASA Apprentice Field Guide qualification at the end rather than a certificate of attendance. The hands can ruin it in the most serious sense on this map: rifle handling and approaching big game on foot are assessed because the failure mode is somebody dying.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, more completely than almost anywhere here. You live in unfenced bush camps with the same cohort for two months to a year, which is the compagnon's house rather than a classroom. The trails-guide ladder above the field-guide qualification means there is always somebody a stage ahead in camp, and somebody a stage behind.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and both East and Southern African entries are settled by the landowners rather than by a school. In Kenya, the Maasai Mara Wildlife Conservancies Association has 24 member conservancies bringing together over 15,000 landowners across about 450,000 acres, with lease fees paid to those landowners annually — the ground itself is a working institution run by the people from it. The South African case is the same shape: the Makuleke community's settlement agreement of 30 May 1998 restored their ownership of the Pafuri land inside Kruger — the first time a community's land rights were restored inside a South African national park — and the Makuleke Contractual Park is co-managed with SANParks.

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. FGASA publishes a genuine ladder — Apprentice Field Guide, Professional Field Guide, Trails Guide, and the trails qualifications above that — and it is one of the better-defined professional routes on this map. Whether the elders you would need are actually in camp, and for how long, is exactly what a fifty-five-day brochure cannot tell you.

sailing-and-yachtmaster.verdict: The one qualification on this map you can genuinely fail, examined by somebody who did not teach you — and we cannot name a single instructor who would get you there

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Empty in all three places. Four RYA centres on the Solent, one school in Auckland, two in Tortola, and not one named instructor between them. That is partly the shape of the thing: the RYA writes the syllabus, licenses the centre and appoints the examiner, so the instructor is deliberately interchangeable. But you will live aboard with this person for a week or sixteen, which makes it a fair question to ask before you book.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open, and the strongest door on this map. UKSA's sixteen-week residential programme takes a novice to a commercially endorsed Yachtmaster; Hamble Point runs a five-day prep and exam. What matters is what the exam is: the Yachtmaster is a Certificate of Competence, assessed by an RYA examiner who is not your instructor, and people fail it. Almost nothing else on this map is marked by somebody with no stake in passing you.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, and closer than anywhere else here — you sleep aboard with a handful of crew and stand watches with them. UKSA's sixteen-week cohort moves together from novice to ticket, which is a ladder in both directions inside one programme, and the BVI liveaboard courses draw a cohort from several continents.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and the Solent settles it twice over. Cowes Week sailed its bicentenary regatta in 2026 with 35 classes racing, and the regatta is already advertising 31 July to 6 August 2027 at the start of its third century — a town whose calendar has been built around sailing for two hundred years. And the Royal Yachting Association, the body that writes the Yachtmaster scheme, has its head office at Hamble-le-Rice, the second town on this page.

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. The ladder is public and unusually clear — Competent Crew, Day Skipper, Coastal, Yachtmaster Offshore, Yachtmaster Ocean — and the sea miles between the rungs are counted rather than claimed. What none of that shows is whether the Solent keeps you after the ticket, which is the difference between a qualification and a place.

ski-touring-and-splitboard.verdict: Three ranges where the craft is the local trade, guided by IFMGA professionals nobody has named — and the fifth answer here is buried under snow rather than unknown

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Empty in all three places. Chamonix's entry named the Compagnie des Guides, founded in 1821, which is a company and not a person, and it has been moved to where the craft comes from; Utah and Lyngen name nobody, though both advertise IFMGA and AMGA certification. In a craft where the guide's judgement in avalanche terrain is the entire product, the name and the certification of the person deciding the route is the question to ask, and every one of these operators can answer it.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open on published dates at every level. The six-day Chamonix-to-Zermatt Haute Route, a three-day ski and splitboard mountaineering camp in the Wasatch, AIARE Level 1 with two field days, Saturday-to-Saturday guided weeks in Lyngen with boat access. And the hands can ruin it in the way that matters most on this map: the skill being taught is choosing where to put your skis on a loaded slope, and the failure mode is an avalanche.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes. Hut-to-hut on the Haute Route you are roped to the people you are learning with; AIARE field days are run in small groups digging the same pit. The Wasatch carries a dense avalanche-course cohort every winter, with professional-level training running alongside the recreational courses — which is what someone above you looks like.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and the Swiss Army settles it for the Chamonix-Verbier half of this page. The Patrouille des Glaciers is run by the Swiss Army every two years: the Z race climbs from Zermatt to Verbier via Arolla, the A race from Arolla to Verbier. The 2026 edition was raced in April and the site is already counting to 2028. A national army putting a ski-mountaineering race across this ground, decade after decade, is the craft belonging to the place rather than visiting it.

evidence.what: the Patrouille des Glaciers, organised by the Swiss Army, on its own races and routes

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. AIARE's levels and the IFMGA guide certification are both published ladders with outside bodies behind them, and the Haute Route is a named thing you could set out to earn. But the ceiling in this craft is measured in seasons of snowpack, and no page publishes whether the people who could teach you that are still there in March.

sound-healing.verdict: The weakest entry on this map, and we would rather say so than dress it up — real cohorts, real certificates, and nothing underneath them that we could check

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Empty in all three places, and there is no honest way to fill it. This map fills this question for a body-taught craft on a named institution with a named lineage — that is how wine and lymphatic drainage are graded. Sound healing has neither: the record's own line on this craft is that there is no single global body, and no individual teacher is named in Kathmandu, the Bay Area or Glastonbury. That is an absence, not a refusal to name.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: This is the one door on the map that does not hold. The dates and the enrolment are real — ten-day trainings in Kathmandu and Pokhara, a 186-hour certificate in Sausalito, diploma routes in the UK — so the first half is a plain yes. The second half is what fails: this question also asks whether your hands can ruin the work, because if they cannot, you are watching a demonstration rather than learning a craft. Nothing you can do to a singing bowl in ten days is wrong in a way anybody could show you. Weigh that against what the certificate costs.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, and this is the honest strength here. The trainings are residential and run as cohorts — ten days and nine nights in Pokhara, 186 hours in Sausalito, a year-long programme at CIIS — so there are people learning beside you, and the diploma routes in the UK have assessors above you.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: No, or at least nothing we could establish. Kathmandu has a genuine metal-bowl-making trade in Patan and Bhaktapur going back centuries, and that is a real craft alive in a real place — but it is a metalworking trade, not this practice, and everything published about it that we could find is published by people selling bowls. Sound healing as taught here would make the same sense in any other town, which is what this question is for.

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been, and unusually there is no published ladder to point at either. This craft's own record says no single global body defines the rungs, so there is nothing above the certificate that an outside authority has described.

spearfishing.verdict: The oldest hunt on earth, and on this map mostly sold as a charter — a state diploma at one end, a guide and a boat at the other, nobody named at either, and one coast where the sport plainly lives

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Empty in all three places, and the page says so about itself: no single named regional club could be verified on the Côte d'Azur. Kona and Cabo name schools and charter operations rather than instructors. This craft is passed between hunters more than it is taught in classes, which makes the absence understandable and does not make it less of a gap.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open, at two very different levels. CREPS PACA at Antibes delivers the French state professional diploma for breath-hold disciplines — a real, examined qualification. Kona Freedivers runs a two-day spearfishing course that requires a Level 1 Freediver certification before you may book it, which is a door with a standard on it. And the hands can ruin it beyond argument: a speargun on a breath-hold, with a shot you either take cleanly or should not take.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Partly, and only in one of the three. France's federated clubs are volunteer associations where members train and qualify together, and a state diploma at Antibes has a cohort by definition. Kona and Cabo sell private charters and one-on-one tours, which is the opposite — good instruction, no bench.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and settled by a federation that is not on this page and sells nothing. The Fédération Française de Pêche Sportive en Apnée ran the Challenge Nicolas Munier off Sainte-Maxime on 25 April 2026, on the Sardinaux plateau — the second round of its French Cup, 22 two-person teams, put on by its own Côte d'Azur regional league and doubling as a qualifier for the national team championship at Frontignan in June. A regional league running a national round on this coast is the sport belonging to the place rather than operating off it. What it does not settle is Kona or Cabo, where we still have nothing but sellers.

evidence.what: the Fédération Française de Pêche Sportive en Apnée on its own Côte d'Azur cup round

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. CMAS grades and the national federation licences are a real ladder, and the French diploma at Antibes is a genuine professional rung. Whether there is a community above you on any of these three coasts, rather than a boat you rent again, is not something a booking page can answer.

surfing.verdict: Five places now, and the two added last are the only two that can tell you who will be in the water with you — the three that have been here longest still cannot

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Empty at three of the five, and the two that answer it are the ones added today. Salt House in Tamraght was founded in 2017 by Yazid Kanane, a surfer from the Souss-Massa region, and its own site calls it 100% Moroccan-owned and operated. Padang Padang Surf Camp has coached the Bukit since 2005, led by Richie, who grew up at Bingin and has coached there over twenty years. Both are people their own schools say do the teaching. Waikiki is still the frustrating one: Hans Hedemann is a former professional with a school under his name, Tony Moniz a Hawaiian professional who founded Faith Surf School in 2000, and the Beachboys have been licensed on that beach since 1955 — and nothing published says whether any of them takes the lesson. Ericeira and Peniche name nobody at all. Two out of five is not a yes; it is a gap with a shape now.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Wide open at every level. Week-long packages on the Waikiki rollers, graded levels one to four at Ericeira with surf guiding above them, residential camps at Peniche running beginners on Baleal's sand, small-group coaching in Tamraght capped at six to a coach, and in Taghazout a four-week route to a Level 1 ISA instructor and lifeguard ticket — the first rung above a holiday that this craft has on the map. And the hands can ruin it in the plainest way on the map: nobody can catch the wave for you, and you will spend the first days failing in front of everybody.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, and Peniche is the clearest ladder here — you can start on the sand at Baleal and end up watching Supertubos in the same corridor, which is someone above you and someone below you in a single town. Ericeira draws Europe's densest surf cohort into camps that are residential by design, and Bali runs the same ladder across one island — the Canggu sand where most of the world's beginners stand up, and the Bukit reefs an hour south where the same coaches take you next.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and settled twice, by two bodies with nothing to sell you. Save The Waves dedicated Ericeira a World Surfing Reserve in October 2011 — the second in the world and the first in Europe, over five kilometres of coastline. And the World Surf League's 2026 Championship Tour holds its tenth event of the year at Supertubos in Peniche, from 16 to 25 October. A world tour and an international conservation designation are the town being part of the sport, rather than a beach with schools on it.

evidence.what: Save The Waves on the Ericeira World Surfing Reserve
the World Surf League's own 2026 event page for Peniche

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. The ISA publishes an instructor and coach ladder, and the progression from whitewater to a green face to a proper turn is real and slow. But surfing's ceiling is measured in years of the same reef in the same season, and whether these towns hold somebody through that is not something a camp advertises.

thai-massage.verdict: A craft the Thai state certifies, UNESCO lists and a Bangkok temple wrote down in stone — the strongest ground on this map, and the only thing missing is anybody of ours on the mat

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Yes, and since 11 September 2026 by name. The Old Medicine Hospital school in Chiang Mai has taught Northern-style Nuad Thai since 1962 under the Ministry of Education, and the school names one of its principal instructors, Ajarn Wasan, in a direct line from its founder Ajarn Sintorn Chaichakan. Wat Pho opened Thailand's first state-recognised traditional medicine school in 1955 and its certificate is recognised by the Ministries of Health, Labour and Education; no individual instructor is named there, and in a ministry-accredited 200-hour programme that is the shape of the thing rather than a hole. ⚠ What ministry recognition is not is an outside examiner. This page used to say it was. The Old Medicine Hospital school assesses its own students against the recognised curriculum and told us so; the claim came off on 11 September 2026. ⚠ Two names have left this page's who-teaches field for where the craft comes from. Asokananda, who founded the Sunshine Network, died in 2005. Chongkol Setthakorn founded ITM and was still leading the morning exercises there in 2019, but founding a school is not teaching your course and nobody has confirmed which he does now. Both names are still on the page, under the heading that is true of them.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open, laddered, and cheap. A 200-hour Professional Thai Massage Therapy course at Wat Pho, a 165-hour professional programme at the Chiang Mai branch, a two-week 60-hour beginner course at Sunshine, six progressive levels at ITM. All published, all accredited, all bookable by a foreigner. And the hands can ruin it: you work with palms, thumbs, elbows and feet on somebody else's spine, and doing it wrong hurts a person.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, and in both directions. Chiang Mai carries a deep community of Thai and international students working through established schools, and ITM's six levels mean the person on the next mat is either a stage ahead of you or a stage behind. This is a craft practised in pairs, so the cohort is not optional — it is the equipment. ⚠ What this page used to say is that the rooms mix Thai and foreign students. The Old Medicine Hospital school corrected that on 11 September 2026: curriculum and language arrangements vary from class to class, so who is on the mat beside you depends on which class you book.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and answered by UNESCO twice rather than by a school. Nuad Thai was inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2019. And the Epigraphic Archives of Wat Pho — 1,431 stone inscriptions cut between 1831 and 1841, among them the massage texts and illustrations in the temple's Twin Pavilion — were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2011. The temple where you would take the course is the place the craft was written down.

evidence.what: UNESCO's Representative List entry for Nuad Thai
UNESCO's Memory of the World entry for the Epigraphic Archives of Wat Pho

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. The rungs are published and long — foundation, therapeutic levels one to four, the 200-hour professional therapy course, and instructor above that — and the Thai ministries stand behind them. Whether there is a teacher above you who would keep taking you further after the certificate is the part no ministry registers.

vipassana-and-meditation.verdict: The most open door on this map and the one that costs nothing — a technique deliberately taught without personalities, in places we could find nobody impartial to describe

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Yes, and in three different forms. Barre publishes five core guiding teachers by name. Igatpuri names nobody on purpose: the Goenka tradition teaches by recorded instruction and appointed assistant teachers, and refusing to build a course around a personality is the tradition's own doctrine rather than our missing research. Yangon carries the Mahasi lineage at the centre Mahasi Sayadaw opened in 1950. ⚠ Our Barre entry named Joseph Goldstein and Sharon Salzberg, whom the school files under its Founders Council rather than among its current teachers — the same error this map made on a pastry school. It is fixed: the page now carries the five the Insight Meditation Society itself names as core guiding teachers — Guy Armstrong, Devin Berry, Kamala Masters, Winnie Nazarko and Carol Wilson — and the two founders sit with the lineage.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open wider than anything else here, and free. The ten-day course runs on published dates worldwide, takes complete beginners, and is given on donation with no fee at all. What the door asks after that is whether you can do it badly, and you can: ten days of noble silence with a fixed timetable is work nobody can do on your behalf, people leave part-way through, and the centres screen applicants because the failure modes are real.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, and at a scale nothing else here matches — Dhamma Giri's pagoda has over four hundred individual cells, and the Mahasi centre in Yangon runs over a hundred buildings for monks, nuns and lay practitioners. The ladder is explicit too: you sit a ten-day course, then you serve one, then you sit the long courses. Somebody above you and somebody below you is built into the structure.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Not established. Igatpuri is the honest problem: the Nashik district government lists Dhamma Giri as a religious site and says nothing more, and everything else published about the town's practice comes from the network that runs the centre. Yangon is almost certainly a yes — Burmese lay meditation is a national practice rather than a visitor's activity — and we could not find a source for it that was not either the centres themselves or a directory of them. Left empty rather than filled on a guess.

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. The ladder here is unusually real and unusually long: ten days, then twenty, thirty, forty-five, and an annual sixty-day course at Dhamma Tapovana, with assistant teacher appointment above all of it. Whether that is a room you would want to be in for years is not a question anybody publishes an answer to, and it is the whole question in this craft.

wildlife-photography.verdict: Named photographers in their own ground, and at the one place we send you the teacher is the operator rather than the man whose name is on the hides — which the page now says

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Yes, and the correction makes it stronger rather than weaker. Bence Máté built over twenty-five hides at Pusztaszer and invented the one-way glass in 2005 — the whole discipline moved because of it — but this page's own entry says the rest out loud: the hides are a facility to hire, not a taught course, and 'Máté himself does not tutor these groups'. The teaching at our pick comes from David Miles, who runs the NaturesLens departures into those hides for a maximum of seven people, and he is now the name in the who-teaches field where Máté used to be. Paul Goldstein has run his own Mara camps for decades and guides the departures himself. Edward Selfe lives in South Luangwa year-round and is a fully qualified guide as well as the photographer teaching you. Lassi Rautiainen is Finland's pioneer of photo-hide tourism and has run Kuhmo since 1988, though what his packages add is guiding rather than tuition. Named people, in their own ground, on the days nobody is watching — and now the right ones.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open, published and priced. Hides let by the night at Pusztaszer, bear and wolf hides at Kuhmo from €210 shared, a seven-night Hungarian hide holiday at £4,499, six-night Mara departures capped at ten, South Luangwa set departures capped at four, and a three-year degree at Falmouth for anybody who wants the long route. And the hands can ruin it twice over: you miss the frame, and worse, you can spook the animal for everybody in the hide.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, though quietly. A hide holds one to five people and the field trips cap at four to twelve, which is small rather than empty, and the people in them run from keen amateurs with a long lens to working professionals — both directions, in one vehicle. Falmouth adds the other kind of cohort entirely, with three year-groups of it.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and Hungary settles it through the national park rather than the hides. The Kiskunság National Park directorate publishes that the Pusztaszer Landscape Protection Area covers 22,225 hectares, of which five thousand are internationally recognised wetland under the Ramsar Convention, with over 280 bird species recorded around its lakes. The birds are there because the ground is protected, not because somebody built a hide. Kenya is the same shape: the Mara conservancies are 24 member conservancies over about 450,000 acres, leased from more than 15,000 Maasai landowners.

That summit is real — Bence Máté is the only photographer to have held both the young and the adult title — but a prize is not a set of rungs, and only somebody who came back to the same animals over years can say whether the ceiling here is worth them.

windsurfing-and-wing-foil.verdict: Eight places chosen for their wind and one instructor named across all of them — the teaching is standardised, the towns genuinely are not

conditions.n: Is there a teacher, and can we name them?
conditions.t: Almost empty, and the exception proves the point. Alan Cadiz at Hawaiian Sailboarding Techniques on Maui is the only instructor named across eight places, and nothing published tells us whether he takes the lessons himself. The other seven — Tarifa, Pozo, Lo Stagnone, Dahab, Naxos, Karpathos and the Californian coast where the board was invented — name nobody. VDWS licenses the school rather than the person, which is why, and it is still worth asking who will be on the beach with you.

conditions.n: Can a stranger get in, on a date you can book?
conditions.t: Open everywhere, cheaply, at every level. VDWS windsurf and wing courses with rental at ION Club centres across four countries, improvement clinics at Pozo, gear-size swapping on weekly and monthly rentals at Dahab. The progression is unusually well-served: shallow standable lagoons at Naxos and Lo Stagnone for a first week, nuclear wind at Pozo and Karpathos for the tenth. And the hands can ruin it — nobody sails your board.

conditions.n: Will there be other people learning beside you?
conditions.t: Yes, and Maui is the clearest case of it anywhere on this map: Kanaha's flatwater nursery and Ho'okipa's wave are the same launch, so a beginner and a world champion share a car park. Karpathos is the other kind — the record's own line is that the windsurf community is the entire scene there, which is a bench with nothing else on it.

conditions.n: Is the craft alive in this place, or is the school the only thing here?
conditions.t: Yes, and the tour settles it. The Professional Windsurfers Association's own 2026 calendar puts a five-star wave World Cup on Gran Canaria from 4 to 12 July and the Aloha Classic on Maui from 19 to 30 October — two of the eight places on this page hosting world-tour events in a single season, booked by nobody who teaches on them. The calendar names the islands rather than the beaches, so it carries Gran Canaria and Maui and does not by itself carry Pozo Izquierdo or Ho'okipa.

evidence.what: the PWA World Tour's own 2026 calendar

conditions.n: Is there enough here to keep you learning for years?
conditions.t: Nobody of ours has been. VDWS and the IWO publish licence levels through to instructor, which is a genuine outside ladder, and the step from sail to wing is a second one most of these towns can teach. What a published level cannot show is whether a place holds you past the season you learned in, and that is the question here.
